opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the main idea with Small was that we didn't want a collection of separate specialized models anymore. For a while we had different models for different things: one more focused on reasoning, one for vision, one for coding. That's fine for experimentation, but for people actually deploying these models it's a pain. You have to route between them, maintain several endpoints, and you get inconsistent behavior depending on which model handles the request. So the goal was really one model that can do all of it reasonably well.

The challenge is that these capabilities interact. When you add a lot of reasoning data, you can make the model very verbose, which hurts when someone just wants a quick answer. When you add multimodal data, you have to make sure you're not degrading text performance. And coding and agentic tool use have their own formatting constraints. A lot of the work is figuring out the data mixture, and doing it carefully at each stage, pretraining, mid-training, and post-training, so one skill doesn't cannibalize another.

One thing that helped a lot was making reasoning something you can control instead of something that's always on. The model can think longer when the problem requires it, like math, hard code, or multi-step agent tasks, and answer directly when it doesn't. That lets you combine the strong-reasoning behavior and the fast, cheap behavior in the same weights, which matters a lot at this size, because people run Small locally or at high volume and care about latency.

Evaluation is also a big part of it. When you merge capabilities, you need a very broad eval suite, because otherwise you optimize one benchmark and silently regress somewhere else. We look at a lot of internal evals, not just public benchmarks, and also at real usage patterns, because what customers actually do is often quite different from what the benchmarks measure.

So overall, it's less about one trick and more about a lot of careful iteration on data and training recipes, so you end up with a single model that's a good default for most use cases, and that's the key for a model like Small.

fable-5.1.text:
The way we think about it is that Mistral Small has to be one model that does many things well, rather than a collection of specialists stitched together. The hard part is that the capabilities compete for the same parameters. If you push very hard on code, you can lose some of the conversational quality. If you push very hard on multilingual data, you can lose some reasoning. So a lot of the work is about the data mixture and the order in which you introduce things.

In pretraining we try to get the broad foundation right: text in many languages, code, math, and increasingly image and document data, because vision is now something people expect even from a small model. We spend a lot of time on the proportions. It is not glamorous work, but the mixture decides most of the final behavior. We run many small-scale experiments where we change one ratio at a time and watch what happens to a set of benchmarks, and also to internal evaluations that look more like real usage.

Then in post-training, we are careful not to let one skill dominate. Instruction following, function calling, long context, and safety behavior all need to be trained together, because if you fine-tune them one after the other, the later stages erase the earlier ones. So we build mixed datasets where a single batch contains tool-use examples next to multilingual chat next to code edits. We also do a lot of filtering, because at this size the model cannot afford to learn from noisy examples.

Another principle for us is that a small model should be honest about its limits. We would rather it refuse to hallucinate a function call than produce a plausible wrong one, because people deploy Small in production, often on their own hardware with low latency requirements. So the capabilities have to be reliable, not just impressive on a benchmark.

And finally, we test everything against how the model is actually used. Many of our users run it locally or in agents, so we look at behavior in long tool-calling loops, with system prompts people write in the real world, in French, German, Spanish, not only English. When something breaks there, we go back to the data rather than patching with prompts. That loop is really how the capabilities end up fitting together in one model.

astra-6.text:
The way I think about it is that you want the capabilities to reinforce each other. You want a model that can write code, reason through a problem, and follow instructions, but you also want it to know when a simple, direct answer is enough.

The challenge is balancing those things in a small model. Improving one capability can come at the expense of another, so you have to look at the model as a whole. It’s not just, “Did the coding score go up?” It’s also, “Is it still useful in a conversation? Does it follow what the user actually asked?” That balance is really the goal.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is that you want the capabilities to reinforce each other. Reasoning, coding, following instructions—these are not completely separate problems. But combining them is not simply a matter of mixing all the data together. You have to pay attention to the balance, because improving one capability can sometimes hurt another.

For a small model, that trade-off is especially important. You have a limited capacity, so the quality of the training data and how you combine it matter a lot. The goal is a model that is useful across different tasks while keeping the efficiency that makes a small model attractive.
